title: Red Allen's feeling, singing and peak with Fletcher Henderson
summary: At Stanley Dance's suggestion Jones discusses trumpeters as they come up; he admired Red Allen's soulful, unique sound, finding him greatest with Fletcher Henderson and good with Luis Russell.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Listen, I'll tell you one thing that I
think we might do as we go along. Stanley mentioned it. He said, 'Get Jonah to talk about different guys.' So while we pass trumpet players, speak about them. You know, what did you feel about Red?
I thought he was a good trumpet player. I thought he had good feeling.
So did I. I loved the way he sang, too.
Good soul. Yeah, and he had a little soul in his singing.
Yeah, he did. He had an absolutely unique sound. Nobody sounded like Red Allen.
He had a plaintive kind of a -- oh, complaint in his style, didn't he?

Yeah, he was like -- he didn't have to play strong and he didn't have to play a lot of chords, because he could play eight bars and take down and take up and play another eight bars, you know, and play it.
Oh, he was so beautiful. I followed him all through my life, as I did other guys.
I was going to ask you, I mean the thing was by the time Red got on 52nd Street he had slipped off a little bit from his peak, I think, don't you?
It was when he was with Fletcher that he sounded good.
When he was with Fletcher was when he was great.
He also played some good stuff with Luis Russell.
